headline: The navy with *no sea*
intent: A country that lost its coast in a war it still refuses to accept, told as a map: the shore it had, the war that took it, the court that said no, and the lake where its sailors train today.

post.premise: Bolivia keeps a navy of thousands though it has had no coastline since the 1880s
post.bait: Which country would you give its coast back? 👇

youtube.title: Bolivia navy: the fleet of a country with no sea 🛰️
youtube.description:
Bolivia lost its only coast to Chile in a nineteenth-century war and has spent more than a century asking for it back, in parades, in treaties and in court. Yet it still keeps a navy. This map story shows the shore it once held, how it was taken, and where its sailors actually train today.
Would you give the coast back? Tell us below.

vo.text: In 1879 Chile marched north in the War of the Pacific. Within a few years the coast was Chilean, and Bolivia was landlocked.

beats.direction: Chile lights solid on its name; the coast route recolours into Chile; Bolivia pulses on landlocked

vo.text: Bolivia never accepted it. Every March it marks the Day of the Sea, with parades far from any shore, and in 2018 it took Chile to the World Court, asking for a way back to the ocean. It lost.

beats.direction: pull back to the whole country; flag sticker on the Day of the Sea; the court card lands on lost

card.text: Chile has no duty to negotiate

vo.text: So where does the navy sail? Up here, on Lake Titicaca, nearly 4 kilometres up in the Andes, with around 5,000 sailors and a fleet of patrol boats.

beats.direction: the twist: tighten onto the lake; the lake glows; the pin and the counter on sailors

research.topic: Bolivia lost its Pacific coast to Chile in the War of the Pacific (1879–1884, Treaty of 1904), keeps a navy based on Lake Titicaca and inland rivers, marks the Day of the Sea on 23 March, and lost its 2018 ICJ case asking Chile to negotiate sea access.

myths.reality: It had about 400 km of Pacific coast (the Litoral department, Antofagasta) from independence in 1825 until 1879.

landscape.our_gap: Bolivia-navy clips are talking heads with a flag; nobody draws the lost shore on the satellite map, shows Chile taking it, the court saying no, and then tightens onto the lake where the sailors are.

brit_wotp.title: War of the Pacific (1879–84)
brit_wotp.notes: Chile against Bolivia and Peru, 1879–84; Bolivia lost its coastal province (Antofagasta) and became landlocked; 1904 treaty confirmed Chilean sovereignty.

brit_bolivia.title: Bolivia — Independence and the War of the Pacific
brit_bolivia.notes: Bolivia's Litoral on the Pacific, roughly 400 km of coast, lost to Chile after 1879.

icj2018.title: Obligation to Negotiate Access to the Pacific Ocean (Bolivia v. Chile), Judgment of 1 October 2018
icj2018.notes: The Court found that Chile did not undertake a legal obligation to negotiate a sovereign access to the Pacific Ocean for Bolivia (12 votes to 3).

reuters_icj.title: World Court rules Chile not obliged to negotiate sea access for Bolivia (1 Oct 2018)
reuters_icj.notes: ICJ ruled against Bolivia; Bolivia lost its 400 km coast in the 1879–83 war.

treaty1904.title: Treaty of Peace and Friendship of 1904 between Chile and Bolivia
treaty1904.notes: Signed 20 October 1904; Bolivia recognised Chilean sovereignty over the former Litoral; Chile granted transit rights and built the Arica–La Paz railway.

bbc_navy.title: Bolivia's landlocked navy dreams of the sea (2018)
bbc_navy.notes: Bolivia's navy, about 5,000 personnel, patrols Lake Titicaca and the rivers; the 23 March Día del Mar; the ICJ case.

armada.title: Armada Boliviana — Historia y misión
armada.notes: Official site of the Bolivian Navy: mission, river and lake districts, Lake Titicaca naval base (Tiquina).

wiki_navy.title: Bolivian Navy
wiki_navy.notes: Armada Boliviana, about 5,000 personnel, headquartered in La Paz, bases on Lake Titicaca and the river systems.

wiki_dia.title: Día del Mar
wiki_dia.notes: Day of the Sea, 23 March, commemorating the loss of the coast (Battle of Topáter, 1879).

brit_titicaca.title: Lake Titicaca
brit_titicaca.notes: Elevation about 3,810 m; on the Peru–Bolivia border; the highest large navigable lake.
